29 March
On this day in 1699

On Baisakhi day, Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib

Beforehand, Hukamnamas had been sent to Sikhs all over Hindustan and beyond, asking them to come to Anandpur with their hair unshorn. The hill chiefs, who according to one account had been told of the Guru’s plan, were present in strength. The Guru abolished the corrupt and debased institution of the masands, created a small regular army and fortified Anandpur with a ring of smaller forts around it.

29 March brings together four moments of Sikh history, from 1699 to 1922. The main event of the day is from 1699: On Baisakhi day, Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib. Together they span four periods, from Guru Gobind Singh Ji and the Khalsa (1675–1708) to The Gurdwara Reform (Akali) movement (1920–1925). People, places and movements connected with this day include Guru Gobind Singh Ji, Anandpur Sahib, the misl sardars and Amritsar.

Also on this day

  • 1748The Sikhs assembled at Amritsar on Baisakhi day and, by a gurmatta, decided to form the Dal Khalsa by reorganizing over 60 armed jathas (bands) They were grouped into eleven associations (misls) under the overall command of Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, as Nawab Kapur Singh, because of his age, retired from active overall leadership.
  • 1849At a Darbar held at Lahore, the British Government deposed and exiled Maharaja Dalip Singh, the last ruler of Punjab They proclaimed the annexation of the Sikh kingdom to the British Empire, towards which they had been moving steadily and strategically for some time. On this day the Sikh state ceased to exist. The soldiers laid down their arms with tears in their eyes, exclaiming “Aj Ranjit Singh mar gia” (“Today Ranjit Singh has died”): only now did they feel the death of their beloved Maharaja.
  • 1922The Akali Dal was renamed the “Shiromani Akali Dal”

Historical background

Guru Gobind Singh Ji and the Khalsa (1675–1708)

Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji was executed in Delhi in 1675 on Aurangzeb's orders, and his son Guru Gobind Singh Ji became the tenth Guru at the age of nine. From Anandpur and Paonta he led the Sikhs through conflicts with the hill rajas and Mughal governors, created the Khalsa at Vaisakhi in 1699, and in the battles of 1704–1705 lost all four Sahibzade. Before his death at Nanded in 1708 he vested Guruship in the Guru Granth Sahib and the Khalsa Panth.

On this day in this period: 1699 On Baisakhi day, Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib.

Persecution, the Dal Khalsa and Abdali's invasions (1717–1764)

After Banda Singh's death the Mughal governors of Lahore, notably Zakariya Khan and Mir Mannu, put prices on Sikh heads, and many Sikhs, such as Bhai Mani Singh and Bhai Taru Singh, were executed. The Sikhs organised in jathas, united as the Dal Khalsa in 1748 and resisted the repeated invasions of Ahmad Shah Abdali, who killed thousands of Sikhs in the Vadda Ghallughara of 1762 and blew up Sri Harmandir Sahib, which the Sikhs rebuilt.

On this day in this period: 1748 The Sikhs assembled at Amritsar on Baisakhi day and, by a gurmatta, decided to form the….

Decline of the Lahore Darbar and annexation (1840–1849)

After Ranjit Singh's death in 1839, the Lahore Darbar was torn by the murders of three successive rulers and court intrigue under the Dogra ministers. The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46) and the Second (1848–49) ended with the British annexation of Punjab in 1849 and the exile of the young Maharaja Duleep Singh.

On this day in this period: 1849 At a Darbar held at Lahore, the British Government deposed and exiled Maharaja Dalip….

The Gurdwara Reform (Akali) movement (1920–1925)

Sikhs organised the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (November 1920) and the Shiromani Akali Dal (December 1920) to free historic gurdwaras from hereditary mahants backed by the government. Through non-violent morchas, including Nankana Sahib (1921), the keys agitation (1921–22), Guru ka Bagh (1922) and Jaito (1923–25), and alongside the militant Babbar Akali movement, the campaign led to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.

On this day in this period: 1922 The Akali Dal was renamed the “Shiromani Akali Dal”.

People and places of this day

Guru Gobind Singh Ji

The tenth Guru (1666–1708), born at Patna. He created the Khalsa in 1699, led the Sikhs through the battles of Anandpur, Chamkaur and Muktsar, composed works collected in the Dasam Granth, and before his death at Nanded vested Guruship in the Guru Granth Sahib.

Read more → · Mentioned on 24 other days of the year

Anandpur Sahib

The town founded by Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji in 1665 as Chak Nanaki, where Guru Gobind Singh Ji created the Khalsa at Vaisakhi in 1699. Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib stands there, and the town hosts Hola Mohalla every year.

Read more → · Mentioned on 14 other days of the year

The misl sardars

The leaders of the Sikh confederacies of the 18th century, such as Nawab Kapur Singh, Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, Baghel Singh and Baba Ala Singh of Patiala. Organised as the Dal Khalsa, they resisted the Afghans and in 1783 Baghel Singh's forces entered Delhi and marked the Sikh historical sites there.

Mentioned on 26 other days of the year

Amritsar

The city founded by Guru Ram Das Ji around the sacred pool of Amritsar. As the home of Sri Harmandir Sahib and the Akal Takht it has been the spiritual and political centre of the Sikhs for four centuries.

Read more → · Mentioned on 69 other days of the year

Maharaja Ranjit Singh

The founder of the Sikh Empire (1780–1839). He took Lahore in 1799, was proclaimed Maharaja in 1801, unified the misls, built a modern army, and covered Sri Harmandir Sahib in gold, giving it the name Golden Temple.

Read more → · Mentioned on 32 other days of the year

Maharaja Duleep Singh

The last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire (1838–1893), youngest son of Ranjit Singh. Deposed at the age of ten when Punjab was annexed in 1849, he was taken to England, later tried to return to India and reclaim his heritage, and died in Paris.

Mentioned on 18 other days of the year

Lahore

The historic capital of Punjab, where Guru Arjan Dev Ji was martyred (Gurdwara Dera Sahib) and Maharaja Ranjit Singh ruled the Sikh Empire from the Lahore Fort. After 1947 it became part of Pakistan.

Mentioned on 49 other days of the year

The Akali movement and its morchas

The Gurdwara Reform movement of 1920–1925, in which jathas of Akali volunteers non-violently took control of historic gurdwaras from mahants. Its campaigns included the keys morcha, Guru ka Bagh and Jaito; tens of thousands were arrested and hundreds killed or injured before the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925. The Shiromani Akali Dal has remained the main Sikh political party.
